tagline: Tree-covered roads link tidal creeks with dunes and Atlantic beaches.
intro: The Ormond Scenic Loop and Trail makes a 34-mile double loop through coastal Florida, with rivers, creeks, marshes, dunes and beaches in the roadway view. Tree canopy covers parts of North Beach Street, Old Dixie Highway and Walter Boardman Lane. Florida Scenic Highways highlights the contrast between tidal creeks, scrub vegetation and a long stretch of undeveloped Atlantic beach. The route holds both Florida Scenic Highway and National Scenic Byway designations.

The modern loop joins roads with earlier identities. Its western leg, County Road 4011, once belonged to U.S. 1. John Anderson Drive was part of a Miami-to-Jacksonville highway absorbed into the Dixie Highway around 1915. The assembled scenic corridor received state designation in July 2007 and national designation in October 2009.

A circuit from The Casements in Ormond Beach crosses the Halifax River on Granada Boulevard, then follows the western leg north through Tomoka State Park toward Bulow Creek State Park. Walter Boardman Lane and Highbridge Road lead east to the Intracoastal Waterway and A1A. From Ormond-by-the-Sea, A1A returns south toward Ormond Beach; John Anderson Drive forms the loop’s central leg. A1A also carries the scenic route north to the Volusia–Flagler county line; North Peninsula State Park lies beside the northern crossing.

moments.title: The Casements
moments.text: The Casements takes its name from its many casement windows, designed to help cool the house. Built in 1913 for the Reverend Dr. Harwood Huntington, the mansion became John D. Rockefeller’s winter home after he bought it in 1918. Rockefeller became known locally for giving dimes to neighbors and visitors. During a golf game, he even handed tire manufacturer Harvey Firestone a dime in recognition of a particularly good shot. The house overlooks the Halifax River and now serves as a city-owned cultural center and park. Its restored riverfront gardens include citrus trees, a promenade, streams and small bridges.

moments.title: Tomoka State Park
moments.text: At Tomoka State Park, the riverbank holds the site of Nocoroco, a Timucuan village. Alvaro Mexia visited in 1605 on an expedition for the Spanish governor. The archaeological record includes a midden made largely of dark earth with pockets of shell, unlike the mostly shell middens common in the region. These deposits help archaeologists document the lives of the people who lived here. The land became a state park in 1945. Frederick Dana Marsh’s Tomokie Fountain marks the village site; the sculpture interprets a legend, rather than depicting a documented event.

moments.title: Bulow Creek State Park
moments.text: The Fairchild Oak is more than four centuries old, part of one of the largest remaining stands of southern live oak on Florida’s east coast. It stands in Bulow Creek State Park on Old Dixie Highway, five miles north of Ormond Beach. The park has nature trails and a picnic pavilion. For a longer excursion, the Bulow Woods Trail runs more than six miles to Bulow Plantation Ruins Historic State Park.
